Senses.Explanation: The transient-guest quarters are the monastery's office and lodging for newly arrived or short-stay monks, supplied with beds and provisions and governed by arrival rules. The Pure Rules orders the guest prefect to keep the quarters' bedding, lamps, firewood, and charcoal ready and to treat new arrivals warmly. Other regulations direct a transient guest to ask where the quarters are, unload there, and meet the guest prefect. Lamp biographies use the same institution in arrival narratives: monks meet or fight there, and the rules for new arrivals determine whether they remain. References to the transient-guest hall and its three-day stay retain the same institutional referent.

Senses.Explanation: Broken tiles and rubble (瓦礫) are discarded fragments of roof tile and masonry. The records use the literal debris in comparisons—“recognizing objects as seeing” is likened to holding rubble, and the question “rubble has no mind; should it also be the Way?” tests an inference from (無心). Public addresses also pair rubble with walls, light, radiance, or gold: “When released, rubble shines; when held fast, gold loses its colour” (放行也瓦礫生煇，把住也黃金失色) explicitly contrasts shining rubble with gold losing colour. The concrete material remains the referent in both literal and evaluative uses.

Senses.Explanation: The Mirror of Qin is a named mirror repeatedly brought into Chan verse and exchange as an instrument before which a form, a speaking participant, or the person himself is exposed and distinguished. In the Recorded Sayings of Master Baiyu, Baiyu Jingsi says that before the mirror a jackal has no way to hide its original form; in the Recorded Sayings of Konggu Daocheng, Konggu Daocheng hangs the mirror at the head of a staff and says that every dust-mote land becomes responsive. In direct questioning recorded in the Recorded Sayings of Master Hansong, Hansong Zhicao answers after the absence of the mirror prompts the question how one can distinguish the matter. The compilers Jing and Yun, narrating Xuefeng Yicun's biography in the Zutang Collection, place Xuefeng face-to-face with the mirror and tell him to inspect himself. These are observable uses of the mirror in appraisal and exposure, not a claim that every mention carries one secret fixed meaning. The headword occurs 29 times in 25 texts in the corpus.

Senses.Explanation: The formula closes an address by directing the assembly to inspect the teaching just enacted before them. Senior seats, rectors, and closing-hammer officers utter it after the presiding teacher’s address. One presiding teacher puts the same formula into the firm-earth deity’s praise after a staff display, showing that the line certifies the completed presentation rather than defining its content.
